newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian air fares poised to rise on fuel costs.
newsitem.headline: Asian air fares poised to rise on fuel costs.

text.p: Asian retail air fares are likely to rise before the end of the year due to sustained high jet fuel costs, industry sources said on Friday.

"What they (airlines) will do is reduce the amount of discount given," said Declan Magee, regional aviation analyst with HG Asia in Hong Kong. They could also reduce the number of discounted tickets available on each flight, he added.
But airlines were not likely to raise published air fares as these were generally about 30 percent more than discounted retail fares, the sources said.
Airlines sell tickets to agents at a discount to the published rates. They can reduce the discounts during peak demand or following increased operating costs, industry sources said.
"Fares in Asia are not even up to published level. There is some way for it (retail fares) to come around," Michael Tan, commercial manager Singapore, Qantas and British Airways Plc, said.
Airlines may add a fare surcharge to offset higher fuel costs during the year-end peak demand period, Tan said.
Peak period fares were usually between three to five percent higher than in low periods, Tan Cheng Beng, Singapore Airlines manager passenger marketing, said.
But he said airlines would monitor traffic carefully before raising prices.
Magee said that although passenger tariff growth had been strong, prices had generally fallen by between one and two percent per annum due to competition and cost savings passed on to the consumer.
"Increasing air fares will not actually address your problem, because if I cannot stimulate travel it will not protect the profitability," Tan Cheng Beng said.
The airlines would not be able to pass on the full increase of fuel prices to consumers and would have to absorb part of it, Magee said.
Analysts said that for the coming financial year airlines' earnings would be strained due to the higher fuel costs.
BA, one of the world's largest airlines, was raising full, published fares on its European routes by 2.5 percent on average from the middle of October due to high fuel costs.
Other European carriers said they were also considering fare hikes to the European routes.

Japan Air System Co Ltd, operating mainly domestic flights, said it was also considering air fare hikes. "If jet fuel prices go up higher, we're afraid the air fare hikes will be unavoidable," a spokesman said.

In its daily circular on Friday, Fraser Securities said in reference to the BA move: "For some of the Asian airlines...we expect similar price adjustments to take place on selected routes, especially for the coming year-end peak travel season.
"Asian airlines have been hit in recent times by escalated fuel prices, up by more than 20 percent since the middle of June 1996.

"Jet fuel prices in Singapore, which act as a benchmark for other regional markets, averaged US$22.80 per barrel in 1995. (They have) been hovering around the US$30.00 per barrel mark since late August this year."
Prices have risen sharply over the past few months as a result of low heating oil stocks in the United States and Europe, tension in the Middle East and rising winter demand.
Fuel purchases make up about 15 percent of an airline's costs.
